power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Ethical approval: Not applicable.
This paper presents a theoretical framework and critiques previously published literature and did not involve the recruitment of human participants.

Lived experience is increasingly recognised alongside clinical, professional and academic expertise, challenging assumptions about whose perspectives are credible in shaping practice, research and policy (Fricker, 2007; Greenhalgh et al., 2016; Sonuga-Barke et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Lived experience is increasingly recognised alongside clinical, professional and academic expertise, challenging assumptions about whose perspectives are credible in shaping practice, research and policy <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fricker, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Greenhalgh et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Sonuga-Barke et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Within autism research, autistic researchers and community members have called for meaningful involvement in determining research priorities, shaping methodological approaches and interpreting findings, highlighting the importance of research that reflects the experiences, needs and priorities of autistic people themselves (Fletcher-Watson et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Within autism research, autistic researchers and community members have called for meaningful involvement in determining research priorities, shaping methodological approaches and interpreting findings, highlighting the importance of research that reflects the experiences, needs and priorities of autistic people themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Fletcher-Watson et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These developments also reflect wider commitments to children's rights, disability justice, and epistemic justice, as well as growing expectations from research funders that people and communities should influence the research that affects them.

Children and young people (CYP) are therefore increasingly understood not simply as recipients of services but as knowledge holders and experts in their own lives, capable of contributing to research design, interpretation and translation (Fletcher-Watson et al., 2025; Lundy & McEvoy, 2012; Sonuga-Barke et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Children and young people (CYP) are therefore increasingly understood not simply as recipients of services but as knowledge holders and experts in their own lives, capable of contributing to research design, interpretation and translation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fletcher-Watson et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lundy & McEvoy, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Sonuga-Barke et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Co-production with CYP has demonstrated what becomes possible when participation extends beyond consultation.

Youth advisory groups, creative participatory methods, co-produced self-report measures and sustained partnerships can enable young people to influence priorities, methods and interpretation, particularly when researchers invest in accessible communication, long-term relationships and shared decision-making (Kakoulidou et al., 2024; Lukito et al., 2025; Pavlopoulou, 2020).
text.formatted: Youth advisory groups, creative participatory methods, co-produced self-report measures and sustained partnerships can enable young people to influence priorities, methods and interpretation, particularly when researchers invest in accessible communication, long-term relationships and shared decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kakoulidou et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lukito et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Pavlopoulou, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These developments are important advances.

The argument developed here is not that participatory research has failed, but that its next methodological challenge is to examine more closely how participation is experienced and how those experiences affect the evidence that research is able to produce.
This paper addresses that challenge by developing the Experience-Sensitive Method of Inquiry (ESMI) for participatory and translational research with CYP, with relevance to CYP with SEND.

The argument proceeds through three linked limitations in current knowledge production (epistemic, participatory and experiential) before setting out eight experience-sensitive dimensions, participatory reflexivity, and the Agency, Belonging and Collaboration (ABC) heuristic through which ESMI can be enacted in practice.

This dual focus is central to ESMI: research should be more responsive and less burdensome for CYP with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) while also generating evidence that better reflects their experiences.
These are linked methodological aims rather than a trade-off between participant wellbeing and scientific quality; whether specific adaptations improve either outcome requires evaluation.

The paper advances a transdisciplinary proposition: improving research encounters is not separate from scientific rigour, because participants' experiences of methods can affect engagement, measurement, missingness and the interpretation of findings.

Across trials, cohorts, Delphi studies, experimental and qualitative inquiry, ESMI invites researchers to examine these relationships from research inception through dissemination, while respecting design-specific requirements for validity, standardisation and comparability.
Scientific methods do not merely record experience; they determine what becomes available as evidence.
Recent evidence has highlighted that across a range of domains and SEND types (Cheng et al., 2025; Palikara et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent evidence has highlighted that across a range of domains and SEND types <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cheng et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Palikara et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Zhang et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Wang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the growing recognition of lived experience, it remains unevenly embedded within the core production of scientific evidence.

CYP may help identify priorities, advise on materials, refine interventions or support dissemination, yet they are less consistently involved in defining constructs, shaping measures, interpreting findings and determining what conclusions should be drawn (Fletcher-Watson et al., 2025; Pavlopoulou et al., 2026; Sonuga-Barke et al., 2024).
text.formatted: CYP may help identify priorities, advise on materials, refine interventions or support dissemination, yet they are less consistently involved in defining constructs, shaping measures, interpreting findings and determining what conclusions should be drawn <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fletcher-Watson et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Pavlopoulou et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Sonuga-Barke et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In this sense, lived experience may inform research without becoming constitutive of the evidence itself.

Across health, education, employment and implementation research, largescale longitudinal studies, intervention trials and national cohort studies continue to rely heavily on standardized psychometric instruments and researcher-defined outcome measures.

These approaches are indispensable for estimating prevalence, evaluating interventions, and identifying population trends (Connelly & Platt, 2014; Fraser et al., 2013; Lombardo et al., 2026; Palikara et al., 2026; Williamson et al., 2012).
text.formatted: These approaches are indispensable for estimating prevalence, evaluating interventions, and identifying population trends <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Connelly & Platt, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Fraser et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Lombardo et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Palikara et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Williamson et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: However, the use of predetermined constructs raises questions about whose knowledge and priorities define what is measured (Greenhalgh et al., 2016; Fricker, 2007).
text.formatted: However, the use of predetermined constructs raises questions about whose knowledge and priorities define what is measured <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Greenhalgh et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Fricker, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Such approaches can also count the population without capturing how they understand their own circumstances (see Lombardo et al., 2026, for  This matters particularly when CYP communicate, process or make meaning of information in ways that differ from the assumptions embedded in conventional measures.
text.formatted: Such approaches can also count the population without capturing how they understand their own circumstances (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Lombardo et al., 2026, for</ref>  This matters particularly when CYP communicate, process or make meaning of information in ways that differ from the assumptions embedded in conventional measures.

text.text: Experiences such as belonging, safety, sensory wellbeing, identity, fatigue, friendship, participation and everyday flourishing are reduced to predefined categories -often without capturing the multidimensionality of these phenomena -or at worst remain absent altogether.

We are not arguing against standardised methods, rather, we believe that standardised measures coexist with an important epistemic limitation: they may identify whether CYP meet researcher-defined constructs without fully capturing what matters most from CYP's own perspectives (Fletcher-Watson et al., 2025; Lukito et al., 2025; Pellicano et al., 2014).
text.formatted: We are not arguing against standardised methods, rather, we believe that standardised measures coexist with an important epistemic limitation: they may identify whether CYP meet researcher-defined constructs without fully capturing what matters most from CYP's own perspectives <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fletcher-Watson et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lukito et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Pellicano et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The consequences are not merely conceptual, but translational too.
The responsiveness of evidence-informed policy and practice is necessarily shaped by the nature and quality of the evidence on which they are based.

If children's experiences are underrepresented, represented mainly through proxy accounts, or elicited through methods that privilege neurotypical ways of communicating and knowing, implementation may reproduce the inequalities it aims to address and reduce (Fricker, 2007; Oliver, 1992).
text.formatted: If children's experiences are underrepresented, represented mainly through proxy accounts, or elicited through methods that privilege neurotypical ways of communicating and knowing, implementation may reproduce the inequalities it aims to address and reduce <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fricker, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Oliver, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Methods of inquiry must therefore be sufficiently sensitive to lived experience for experiential knowledge to shape what counts as evidence from the outset.
Research involving CYP with SEND makes these challenges particularly visible.

SEND is an important policy framework for educational entitlement and support, but it is not a homogeneous category; it encompasses highly diverse cognitive, communicative, sensory, physical, emotional and learning experiences (Department for Education & Department of Health, 2015; Education Committee, 2025).
text.formatted: SEND is an important policy framework for educational entitlement and support, but it is not a homogeneous category; it encompasses highly diverse cognitive, communicative, sensory, physical, emotional and learning experiences (Department for Education & Department of Health, 2015; Education Committee, 2025).

text.text: Treating CYP with SEND as a single, homogeneous population risks overlooking the considerable diversity of their experiences, needs, and forms of communication.
It may also reinforce deficit-based assumptions that equate disability or difference with reduced competence, participation, or ability to contribute (Botha, 2021; Oliver, 1992).
text.formatted: It may also reinforce deficit-based assumptions that equate disability or difference with reduced competence, participation, or ability to contribute <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Botha, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Oliver, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: These assumptions can shape whose perspectives are recognised as legitimate sources of evidence.

Where communication differs from neurotypical expectations, researchers may rely disproportionately on parents, teachers or professionals to interpret or represent CYP experiences despite evidence of discrepancies between first person and proxy reported accounts across neurodevelopmental populations (Alamolhoda et al., 2021; Berástegui et al., 2021 , Sheldrick et al., 2012; Skaletski et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Where communication differs from neurotypical expectations, researchers may rely disproportionately on parents, teachers or professionals to interpret or represent CYP experiences despite evidence of discrepancies between first person and proxy reported accounts across neurodevelopmental populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alamolhoda et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Berástegui et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">, Sheldrick et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Skaletski et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While proxy perspectives can provide valuable contextual information, they cannot substitute for first-person accounts when the focus of inquiry is lived experience.

Consequently, methodological approaches that fail to accommodate diverse forms of communication and participation risk reproducing epistemic exclusion by privileging accounts that align with established research conventions over the first-person experiences of CYP.
Inviting CYP into research does not in itself address epistemic exclusion when the conceptual and methodological architecture of inquiry remains predominantly researcher defined.

Participatory and co-produced research has sought to address this problem by moving from research on CYP towards research with them (Lundy & McEvoy, 2012; Sonuga-Barke et al., 2024; Fletcher-Watson et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Participatory and co-produced research has sought to address this problem by moving from research on CYP towards research with them <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Lundy & McEvoy, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Sonuga-Barke et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Fletcher-Watson et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence from autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) research demonstrates that meaningful partnership can influence research priorities, methods, measures and interpretation of findings (Kakoulidou et al., 2024; Lukito et al., 2025).

The Experience-Sensitive Method of Inquiry (ESMI) is a methodological approach through which lived experience can become constitutive of trustworthy scientific evidence without losing the relational, embodied and contextual qualities that give that experience meaning.
Rather than treating participation as a procedural requirement or ethical aspiration, ESMI positions participation as an epistemological process through which knowledge is produced.
It begins from the premise that the quality of scientific evidence is inseparable from the quality of the research encounters through which that evidence emerges.
ESMI complements existing participatory, inclusive and accessibility-oriented approaches rather than replacing them.

While participatory methodologies have made important contributions to involving CYP in research, involvement alone does not necessarily ensure that experiential knowledge meaningfully influences evidence production.
CYP may be included in studies whose research questions conceptual frameworks, outcome measures and interpretive assumptions remain largely researcher defined.
ESMI builds on these approaches by making the responsiveness of research decisions to participants' experiential knowledge an ongoing focus of methodological reflexivity.
This challenge is particularly relevant in research with CYP with SEND.

text.text: Central to this perspective is the recognition that each person inhabits an irreducibly subjective lifeworld and is therefore the primary authority on their own lived experience.

Humanising practice therefore requires attention not only to observable outcomes but also to how people understand and make sense of their experiences, recognising that these meanings cannot be fully inferred through external observation, diagnostic categories or proxy interpretation.

If only participants have direct access to the meanings of their own lived experiences, then research methods must create the conditions in which those meanings can inform the production and interpretation of scientific knowledge, rather than being displaced by external classifications, assumptions or proxy interpretations.

Sense-making: Recognising CYP as active meaning-makers who interpret and connect experiences within the context of their own lives, relationships and identities.

Strengthens conceptual validity by enabling participants to explain how experiences connect, what they mean and why they matter, rather than reducing evidence to isolated responses or predefined constructs.
CYP are supported to explain experiences in ways that make sense to them and reflect the connections they make across their lives.
Research fragments experience into predefined questions, categories or variables that fail to reflect how participants understand their own lives.
Encourage narrative and visual methods, mapping and timelines, alongside structured methods, with opportunities for collaborative interpretation.
Recognising CYP as people whose identities, experiences and meanings develop across time, shaped by their histories, present circumstances and future possibilities.

Strengthens contextual and interpretive validity by situating participants' accounts within the continuity of their lives, reducing the risk of interpreting experiences as isolated events rather than part of an unfolding personal journey.

Researchers seek to understand who CYP are becoming, recognising that current experiences are shaped by past relationships, significant life events, experiences of exclusion, trauma, masking or being unheard, as well as their hopes for the future.
Research treats participants as decontextualised cases or isolated snapshots rather than people with evolving histories and futures.
Invite reflection on significant experiences, transitions, hopes and anticipated futures through narrative approaches, timelines, life maps or longitudinal engagement where appropriate.
Explore previous educational, healthcare and research experiences before data collection and adapt approaches accordingly.

Sense of place: Recognising that physical, sensory, social and cultural environments shape whether CYP experience research as a place of belonging, familiarity and ease or of dislocation and alienation.

Strengthens ecological validity by creating research environments in which CYP can participate in ways that are authentic to their everyday lives, reducing sensory and cognitive burden and the influence of environmental dislocation on the knowledge produced.

Physical surroundings, routines, relationships and expectations support CYP to experience research as a place where they can comfortably be themselves rather than needing to adapt to unfamiliar institutional norms.
Research environments privilege institutional routines, unfamiliar expectations or sensory demands that leave participants feeling like strangers within the research process.

Consider not only physical accessibility (e.g. lighting, noise, sensory supports, room layout and visually accessible materials) but also the relational and cultural atmosphere created through routines, expectations, communication and opportunities for participants to shape the space.

Embodiment: Recognising that CYP experience, communicate and participate as embodied persons, whose thoughts, emotions, sensory experiences and actions are inseparable from their bodily ways of being in the world.

Strengthens ecological and conceptual validity by recognising embodied experience as a legitimate source of knowledge, reducing the risk that important meanings are overlooked when research privileges verbal, behavioural or reductionist forms of evidence.

Researchers recognise that movement, silence, stimming, sensory regulation, affect, fatigue, posture, pacing and alternative communication are understood as meaningful expressions of participation rather than disruptions to it.
Embodied experiences are overlooked or reduced to behaviours, symptoms or measurement.
Recognise and support diverse embodied ways of participating, including movement, sensory supports, processing time, camera-off participation and AAC or other forms of expression.
Attend to how movement, stillness and other embodied responses may also offer insight into participants' experiences, without imposing predetermined interpretations.

Across all dimensions, researchers are encouraged to engage in ongoing reflexive practice, critically examining how disciplinary assumptions, methodological choices, institutional norms and power relationships influence what becomes visible as evidence and whose knowledge is recognised as legitimate.
The eight experience-sensitive dimensions provide the phenomenological and epistemological foundations of ESMI.

Translating these foundations into research practice requires ongoing attention to how methodological decisions shape the conditions under which experiential knowledge becomes expressible, recognisable and influential.
To support this process, ESMI proposes three interconnected methodological principles: Agency, Belonging and Collaboration (ABC).

These principles provide a practical framework for participatory reflexivity by encouraging researchers to examine how research environments, relationships and practices enable CYP to influence the production of knowledge.
Together the experiencesensitive dimensions and ABC principles seek to understand and strengthen both the quality of participation and trustworthiness of the evidence that emerges from it.

Eight interconnected experience-sensitive dimensions provide the framework's phenomenological and epistemological foundations, while Agency, Belonging and Collaboration (ABC) function as practical, mutually reinforcing principles for methodological decision-making.

Participatory reflexivity operates across these elements, encouraging ongoing examination of how research relationships, environments, assumptions and methodological choices shape participation and knowledge production.
ESMI pursues two linked aims: improving how children and young people with SEND experience research and strengthening the relevance, interpretability and trustworthiness of the evidence produced.
Agency, Belonging and Collaboration (ABC) provides a practical reflexive heuristic for translating experience-sensitive dimensions into methodological actions.
They do not represent separate stages of participation, nor do they simplify the eight dimensions into a smaller framework.
Rather, they function as interconnected principles that support researchers in examining how experiential knowledge becomes expressed, recognised, and influential throughout the research process.
The relationship between the eight dimensions and ABC remains dynamic, nonhierarchical and mutually reinforcing.
Each principle draws on several experience-sensitive dimensions, and each dimension may inform more than one principle.
The methodological focus is on how these relationships shape what can become known.
Within ESMI, Agency concerns whether children and young people can influence the questions, constructs, methods and interpretations through which knowledge is produced.
Supported particularly by the dimensions of agency, insiderness, uniqueness and sensemaking, it requires more than offering choices within predetermined procedures.
Participants' experiential knowledge must be capable of challenging researchers' assumptions and redirecting inquiry.

Agency therefore encourages researchers to examine whose priorities define the research agenda, whose interpretations are privileged and whether participants have meaningful opportunities to influence decisions throughout the research process.
Belonging concerns the relational, sensory, embodied and environmental conditions that enable children and young people to participate as themselves.

The dimensions of togetherness, sense of place, embodiment and personal journey draw attention to how histories of exclusion, expectations of conformity, fatigue or sensory demands and power relationships, whether participants feel welcomed, understood, and able to contribute meaningfully.

These conditions are methodologically consequential because they affect what participants can express and what researchers may mistakenly interpret as disengagement, resistance, lack of capacity or deficit.
Belonging therefore encourages researchers to attend to the conditions through which participation becomes possible and meaningful.
ESMI is not confined to qualitative or explicitly participatory methodologies.

As a methodological orientation, experience-sensitivity can inform quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods research without prescribing a particular design or replacing its established standards.
Instead, it asks how methodological decisions influence what participants can express, how participation is experienced and what becomes recognised as evidence.
The form and degree of involvement will vary by design, and proposed gains in evidence quality require empirical evaluation.
In randomised controlled trials, Agency may inform the selection of outcomes that young people regard as meaningful, alongside the feasibility and acceptability of study procedures.
Belonging may inform accessible recruitment, consent and assessment encounters.
Collaboration may support interpretation of perceived benefits, burdens and implementation implications.
These contributions could strengthen outcome relevance and the interpretation of intervention effects but should be evaluated rather than assumed to improve measurement validity.
In experimental studies, Agency may inform task acceptability and preparation;
Collaboration may contextualise participants' task experiences when interpreting findings.
Adaptations should be considered alongside requirements for experimental control, signal quality, standardisation and comparability.
Researchers should document which elements can be adapted, which must remain consistent, why those boundaries exist and whether proposed adaptations affect measurement integrity.
Experience-sensitivity does not justify relaxing scientific rigour; it creates opportunities to examine how the conditions of testing may themselves shape engagement and the evidence produced.
Young people should be invited to explain how proposed procedures and constraints are experienced, identify burdens or unintended consequences, and suggest alternatives.

Where an adaptation cannot be adopted, researchers should communicate the reasons without implying that the young person's experience is less valid, document the decision, and revisit it when new information emerges.
This process should not transfer responsibility for methodological trade-offs onto young people or promise influence where decisions are already fixed.
Instead, it makes the boundaries of influence transparent and treats disagreement as an opportunity for reciprocal learning.

Any adaptations adopted should still be evaluated for their implications for data quality, standardisation and comparability; these are proposed practices requiring empirical evaluation, not guarantees of improved outcomes.

Across these designs, ESMI invites examination of two linked questions: did the study create a more respectful, accessible and meaningful research experience for this population, and did those conditions improve what could be measured, interpreted or translated?
Neither benefit should be assumed solely from the presence of participatory procedures.
Their interdependence matters.

Agency without belonging may leave participants unable to exercise meaningful choice; belonging without agency may create welcoming encounters without redistributing epistemic influence; and collaboration requires researchers to remain responsive to both.
The relevant question is not simply whether participation occurred, but what it enabled researchers and participants to know.

In SEND research, difficulties with questionnaires, repeated assessments or experimental tasks should prompt examination of possible methodological mismatch, rather than automatic attribution to participant limitations.
Such reflexivity must be balanced with the requirements of measurement validity, standardisation and comparability.

ESMI therefore connects the quality of research encounters to the relevance and trustworthiness of the evidence produced, while recognising that the forms and degree of participation may vary according to the research question and design.

Future evaluation should therefore consider both participant-defined indicators of research experience (including agency, accessibility, sensory burden and whether contributions were consequential) and design-appropriate indicators of evidence quality (such as construct relevance, response patterns, measurement integrity, interpretability and uptake).
The relationship between these outcomes is an empirical question, not an automatic consequence of participation.
The applications outlined above illustrate the potential of ESMI across research designs, rather than providing empirical evidence of its effectiveness.

ESMI offers a transdisciplinary methodological orientation, grounded in Agency, Belonging and Collaboration, that places these considerations at the heart of research design and interpretation.
Further research is needed to evaluate its potential to improve both participants' experiences and the relevance and trustworthiness of the evidence produced.

Collaboration concerns reciprocal knowledge-making across the research lifecycle, including the negotiation of research priorities, interpretations and applications.

Supported particularly by the dimensions of togetherness, insiderness, sense-making and agency, it recognises that participants and researchers bring different but valuable forms of knowledge to the research process.
It does not require agreement or identical levels of co-production in every study.
Instead, it requires openness to experiential expertise that challenges disciplinary assumptions, while making transparent how participants' contributions influence decisions and scientific claims.
Collaboration therefore encourages dialogue, negotiation and shared interpretation, recognising that differences in perspectives can enrich rather than undermine knowledge generation.

They are not sequential stages or a second theoretical framework: agency concerns influence over knowledge production; belonging concerns the conditions for authentic engagement; and collaboration concerns reciprocal interpretation and action.
Collectively, these principles shift the central evaluative questions of participatory research.
Rather than asking simply whether children and young people were involved, ESMI encourages researchers to ask: • Agency: Do young people have genuine influence over the inquiry?
• Belonging: Can young people participate as themselves?
• Collaboration: How is experiential knowledge influencing interpretation and action?

In this sense, the mode through which CYP encounter and participate in inquiry is epistemologically consequential because it shapes what researchers can notice and, ultimately, what can come to count as evidence.

If translational research seeks to improve CYP's lives, the methods through which lived experience becomes evidence deserve the same critical attention as the interventions and policies that emerge from that evidence.

The challenge is therefore not simply to include lived experience, but to enable it to become constitutive of trustworthy evidence without stripping away the relational, embodied and contextual qualities through which it is lived.

This experiential limitation provides a central rationale for ESMI: experience-sensitive inquiry requires researchers to examine not only what methods capture, but also how those methods, and the interactions they create, shape what can be known.

In longitudinal cohort studies, Agency may inform the selection of constructs and repeated measures that matter to participants.

Belonging may support accessible follow-up as needs and circumstances change and Collaboration may help interpret missingness, attrition and developmental patterns without presuming participant deficit.

Experiencesensitive practice may also help researchers examine response consistency, retention and the meaning of change over time, while preserving the comparability required for longitudinal inference.

In Delphi studies, Agency may inform panel composition and the framing of consensus questions; Belonging may require accessible rounds and meaningful routes for dissent; and Collaboration may make visible differences between lived experience and professional judgements rather than treating numerical consensus as the only relevant result.
Researchers should report how accessibility and deliberation shaped the process without assuming that inclusion guarantees consensus or validity.

In qualitative studies, Agency may support participant-led topics and communication choices; Belonging may shape relationally safe and sensory-considerate encounters; and Collaboration may enable participants to question emerging themes and influence how findings are communicated.
Such practices may contribute to interpretive depth, credibility and the authenticity of accounts, while remaining open to disagreement and to the limits of any individual interpretation.

An experience-sensitive conversation about experimental adaptations should be honest, collaborative and accessible, taking account of each CYP's developmental experiences, communication preferences and individual circumstances.

Researchers can use accessible and individually responsive approaches, including Easy Read materials, visual explanations, illustrated scenarios, videos, demonstrations and AAC, to explain what a task is intended to measure, why some procedures need to be similar for everyone, what is known or uncertain about how a proposed change might affect the data, and which options remain open.
Young people should be invited to describe what feels difficult, suggest alternatives and disagree without pressure.
Where a requested adaptation cannot be offered, researchers should explain the reason without presenting the methodological decision as a judgement about the young person's capacity or needs.
They should also make clear that declining or stopping participation remains an acceptable choice.

In experimental research, potential tensions between participants' preferred adaptations and requirements for standardisation, signal quality and comparability should be approached through open, valuesbased conversations rather than framed as a choice between inclusion and rigour.

Drawing on the co-intentional approach described by Sonuga-Barke et al. (2024), researchers and young people can establish shared purposes, recognise the value and limits of different forms of expertise, and discuss disagreements and uncertainties in good faith.

Researchers should explain, in accessible terms, which features of a task are important for answering the scientific question, why they matter, what remains uncertain, and which elements may be negotiated.

The Experience-Sensitive Method of Inquiry (ESMI): Translating experience-sensitive dimensions into methodological considerations for participatory research with children and young people with SEND to strengthen the production of trustworthy scientific knowledge.
